questions.question: தமிழ் எழுத்துக்களின் மொத்த எண்ணிக்கை 247. இதில் உயிர்மெய் எழுத்துக்களின் எண்ணிக்கை எவ்வாறு கணக்கிடப்படுகிறது?
questions.explanation: உயிர்மெய் எழுத்துக்கள் 12 உயிர் மற்றும் 18 மெய் ஆகியவற்றின் பெருக்கல் மூலம் 216 ஆகும்.

questions.question: உயிர் எழுத்துக்கள் 12-ல் குறில் எழுத்துக்கள் எத்தனை, அவற்றின் மாத்திரை அளவு என்ன?
questions.explanation: குறில் எழுத்துக்கள் 5 (அ, இ, உ, எ, ஒ) மற்றும் அவை 1 மாத்திரை அளவு கொண்டவை.

questions.question: மெய் எழுத்துக்களின் வகைப்பாடு மற்றும் அவற்றின் எண்ணிக்கை குறித்து பின்வருவனவற்றுள் எது சரியானது?
questions.explanation: மெய் எழுத்துக்கள் 18-ல் வல்லினம் 6, மெல்லினம் 6, இடையினம் 6 என வகைப்படுத்தப்படுகின்றன.

options: முதல் எழுத்து 12 உயிர் மற்றும் 18 மெய் சேர்ந்த 30 எழுத்துக்கள் ஆகும்.

snapshot.title: TNPSC General Tamil: எழுத்திலக்கணம் (Orthography)
snapshot.exam_hook: 🎯 TNPSC Tamil Hook: Total: 247. Prime: 30. Vowels: 12. Consonants: 18. Consonant Maathirai: 0.5. Long Vowel Maathirai: 2. Sarbu Eluthu types: 10.

quick_notes.title: Tamil Letters: The 247 Map
quick_notes.detail: Uyir Eluthu (Vowels): 12. Mey Eluthu (Consonants): 18. Uyirmey (Vowel-Consonant): 12 × 18 : 216. Ayutha Eluthu : 1. Total : 247 letters.
quick_notes.explanation: தமிழ் எழுத்துக்கள் மொத்தம் 247. இதில் உயிர் எழுத்துக்கள் 12, மெய் எழுத்துக்கள் 18. உயிரும் மெய்யும் சேர்ந்து உயிர்மெய் எழுத்துக்கள் ஆகும்; இவை 12 x 18 = 216. மேலும் ஆய்த எழுத்து ஒன்று உண்டு. ஆக மொத்தம் 12 + 18 + 216 + 1 = 247 எழுத்துக்கள்.

quick_notes.title: Uyir Eluthu (12 Vowels)
quick_notes.detail: Kuril (Short): 5 (அ, இ, உ, எ, ஒ) - 1 Maathirai. Nedil (Long): 7 (ஆ, ஈ, ஊ, ஏ, ஐ, ஓ, ஔ) - 2 Maathirai. Note : ஐ (Ai) and ஔ (Au) are long vowels.
quick_notes.explanation: உயிர் எழுத்துக்கள் பன்னிரண்டு (12) ஆகும். இவை குறில் (short) மற்றும் நெடில் (long) என இரண்டு வகைப்படும். குறில் என்பது ஒரு மாத்திரை (time unit) நேரத்தில் உச்சரிக்கப்படும் ஐந்து எழுத்துக்கள்: அ, இ, உ, எ, ஒ. நெடில் என்பது இரண்டு மாத்திரை நேரத்தில் உச்சரிக்கப்படும் ஏழு எழுத்துக்கள்: ஆ, ஈ, ஊ, ஏ, ஐ, ஓ, ஔ. ஐ (Ai) மற்றும் ஔ (Au) ஆகிய இரண்டும் நெடில் உயிர்கள் ஆகும். ஒவ்வொரு உயிர் எழுத்துக்கும் குறில் அல்லது நெடில் என்ற தன்மை உண்டு.

quick_notes.title: Mey Eluthu (18 Consonants)
quick_notes.detail: Vallinam (Hard): 6 (க், ச், ட், த், ப், ற்). Mellinam (Soft): 6 (ங், ஞ், ண், ந், ம், ன்). Idaiyinam (Medium): 6 (ய், ர், ல், வ், ழ், ள்). Pronunciation time : 0.5 Maathirai.
quick_notes.explanation: தமிழ் மொழியில் உள்ள மெய் எழுத்துக்கள் மொத்தம் 18 ஆகும். இவை மூன்று வகைகளாகப் பிரிக்கப்படுகின்றன: வல்லினம் (கடின ஒலி), மெல்லினம் (மென்மையான ஒலி), இடையினம் (நடுத்தர ஒலி). வல்லின எழுத்துக்கள் ஆறு: க், ச், ட், த், ப், ற். மெல்லின எழுத்துக்கள் ஆறு: ங், ஞ், ண், ந், ம், ன். இடையின எழுத்துக்கள் ஆறு: ய், ர், ல், வ், ழ், ள். இந்த மெய் எழுத்துக்கள் ஒவ்வொன்றும் உச்சரிக்கப்படும் நேரம் அரை மாத்திரை (0.5 Maathirai) என அளவிடப்படுகிறது.

quick_notes.title: Mudal vs Sarbu Eluthu
quick_notes.detail: Mudal Eluthu: 12 Uyir + 18 Mey : 30 prime letters. Sarbu Eluthu (Dependent): 10 types including Uyirmey, Ayutham, Uyiralabedai, Otralabedai, Kutriyalugaram, etc. TNPSC frequently asks "How many Sarbu Eluthu types?" — Answer is 10.
quick_notes.explanation: Mudal Eluthu enpathu mudhalmaiyana ezhuthukkal. Avai 12 Uyir ezhuthukkalum 18 Mey ezhuthukkalum serndha 30 ezhuthukkal aagum. Sarbu Eluthu enpathu sarbu ezhuthukkal, anavadhu marra ezhuthukkalai sarbu pattu varuvai. Ivai 10 vagai – avai Uyirmey, Ayutham, Uyiralabedai, Otralabedai, Kutriyalugaram munbuvana aagum. TNPSC thodarndhu “Sarbu Eluthu ethanai vagai?” enru ketpadhal, vidalai 10 aagum.

quick_notes.title: Maathirai (Time Measure)
quick_notes.detail: Short vowel : 1. Long vowel : 2. Consonant/Ayutham : 0.5. Alabedai (Elongation) : varies. Skill : Be able to calculate total Maathirai for a given word like "தமிழ்" (0.5+1+1 : 2.5).
quick_notes.explanation: மாத்திரை என்பது தமிழில் ஒலியின் நேர அளவைக் குறிக்கும் அலகு ஆகும். குறில் உயிரெழுத்து (அ, இ, உ போன்றவை) ஒரு மாத்திரை நேரம் எடுக்கும். நெடில் உயிரெழுத்து (ஆ, ஈ, ஊ போன்றவை) இரண்டு மாத்திரை நேரம் எடுக்கும். மெய்யெழுத்து (க், ச், த் போன்றவை) மற்றும் ஆய்த எழுத்து (ஃ) ஒவ்வொன்றும் அரை மாத்திரை (0.5) நேரம் எடுக்கும். அலபெடை (ஒலி நீட்டிப்பு) என்பது சொல்லுக்கேற்ப மாறுபடும் மாத்திரை அளவு. உதாரணமாக, "தமிழ்" என்ற சொல்லில் 'த' (மெய்) 0.5, 'மி' (குறில்) 1, 'ழ்' (மெய்) 0.5, 'ல்' (மெய்) 0.5 ஆக மொத்தம் 2.5 மாத்திரை ஆகும்.

quick_notes.title: Sentence Parts (வாக்கிய உறுப்புகள்)
quick_notes.detail: 1. Ezhuvai (Subject): The doer or the main noun (e.g., "தென்றல்" படித்தாள்). 2. Payanilai (Predicate): The action or state (தென்றல் "படித்தாள்"). 3. Seyappaduporul (Object): The receiver of action (தென்றல் "பாடம்" படித்தாள்).
quick_notes.explanation: வாக்கிய உறுப்புகள் என்பது ஒரு வாக்கியத்தில் உள்ள மூன்று முக்கிய பகுதிகள் ஆகும். எழுவாய் (Subject) என்பது வாக்கியத்தின் செயலைச் செய்பவரைக் குறிக்கும், எடுத்துக்காட்டாக "தென்றல் படித்தாள்" இல் 'தென்றல்' எழுவாய். பயனிலை (Predicate) என்பது அவர் செய்த செயலைச் சொல்லும், அதே வாக்கியத்தில் 'படித்தாள்' பயனிலை. செயப்படுபொருள் (Object) என்பது செயலால் பாதிக்கப்படும் பொருளைக் குறிக்கும், எடுத்துக்காட்டாக "தென்றல் பாடம் படித்தாள்" இல் 'பாடம்' செயப்படுபொருள்.

quick_notes.title: Types of Sentences (வாக்கிய வகைகள்)
quick_notes.detail: 1. Seithi (Statement): Simple information. 2. Vinai (Question): Ends with ?. 3. Kattalai (Command): Giving orders. 4. Unarchi (Exclamatory): Expresses emotion. 5. Thanvinai (Self-action), whereas Piravinai (Caused action). 6. Seivinai (Active), whereas Seyappaduvinai (Passive).
quick_notes.explanation: வாக்கிய வகைகள் என்பது நாம் பேசும்போதும் எழுதும்போதும் பயன்படுத்தும் வெவ்வேறு வகை வாக்கியங்களைக் குறிக்கும். முதல் வகை செய்தி வாக்கியம், இது ஒரு தகவலை சொல்லும் வாக்கியம்; உதாரணமாக, "நான் பள்ளிக்கு செல்கிறேன்" என்பது செய்தி. இரண்டாம் வகை வினா வாக்கியம், இது கேள்வி கேட்கும் வாக்கியம், இதன் முடிவில் ? குறி வைக்கப்படும்; உதாரணமாக, "நீ எங்கே போகிறாய்?" என்பது வினா. மூன்றாம் வகை கட்டளை வாக்கியம், இது ஒரு கட்டளையை கொடுக்கும் வாக்கியம்; உதாரணமாக, "உட்கார்" என்பது கட்டளை. நான்காம் வகை உணர்ச்சி வாக்கியம், இது உணர்ச்சியை வெளிப்படுத்தும் வாக்கியம்; உதாரணமாக, "எவ்வளவு அழகு!" என்பது உணர்ச்சி. ஐந்தாம் வகை தன்வினா என்பது தானே செய்யும் செயலைக் குறிக்கும், அதே நேரத்தில் பிறவினா என்பது மற்றவரால் செய்யப்படும் செயலைக் குறிக்கும்; உதாரணமாக, "அவன் ஓடினான்" என்பது தன்வினா, "அவனை ஓட வைத்தான்" என்பது பிறவ

quick_notes.title: Active & Passive (செய்வினை, செயப்பாட்டுவினை)
quick_notes.detail: Seivinai: Subject is active (e.g., கரிகாலன் கல்லணையைக் கட்டினான்). Seyappaduvinai : Focus on object, uses "பட்டது" suffix (e.g., கல்லணை கரிகாலனால் கட்டப்பட்டது).
quick_notes.explanation: செய்வினை என்பது, வாக்கியத்தில் செயலைச் செய்பவராகிய எழுவாய் முக்கியமாக இருப்பது. உதாரணமாக, "கரிகாலன் கல்லணையைக் கட்டினான்" என்பதில் கரிகாலன் என்பவர் செயலைச் செய்தார். செயப்பாட்டுவினை என்பது, செயலைப் பெறும் பொருளாகிய செயப்படுபொருள் முக்கியமாக இருப்பது. இதில் வினைச்சொல்லுடன் "பட்டது" என்ற பின்னொட்டு சேர்க்கப்படும். உதாரணமாக, "கல்லணை கரிகாலனால் கட்டப்பட்டது" என்பதில் கல்லணைதான் முக்கியமானது. இந்த இரண்டு வினை வகைகளும் ஒரே உண்மையை வெவ்வேறு கோணத்தில் சொல்கின்றன.

quick_notes.title: Thanvinai & Piravinai (தன்வினை, பிறவினை)
quick_notes.detail: Thanvinai: Subject does the action (e.g., அவன் படித்தான்). Piravinai : Subject causes someone else to do (e.g., அவன் படிப்பித்தான்). TNPSC loves testing this distinction.
quick_notes.explanation: தன்வினை என்பது, செயலைச் செய்பவரே அந்தச் செயலை நேரடியாகச் செய்வதைக் குறிக்கும். உதாரணமாக, "அவன் படித்தான்" என்பதில் படிப்பவன் அவனே. பிறவினை என்பது, செயலைச் செய்பவர் வேறொருவரை வைத்துச் செய்விப்பதைக் குறிக்கும். உதாரணமாக, "அவன் படிப்பித்தான்" என்பதில் அவன் படிக்கவில்லை, மற்றவரைப் படிக்க வைத்தான். TNPSC தேர்வில் இந்த இரண்டுக்குமான வேறுபாட்டை அடிக்கடி கேட்பார்கள்.

quick_notes.title: Sentence Connectors
quick_notes.detail: How words like எனில், ஆதலால், எனினும் are used to combine simple sentences into complex ones.
quick_notes.explanation: தலைப்பு: வாக்கிய இணைப்பிகள் எளிய வாக்கியங்களை இணைத்து சிக்கலான வாக்கியங்களாக மாற்ற, எனில், ஆதலால், எனினும் போன்ற சொற்கள் பயன்படுத்தப்படுகின்றன. எனில் என்றால் 'if' அல்லது 'என்றால்' என்று பொருள்; இது ஒரு நிபந்தனையைக் காட்டுகிறது. ஆதலால் என்றால் 'because' அல்லது 'எனவே' என்று பொருள்; இது ஒரு காரணத்தையும் அதன் விளைவையும் இணைக்கிறது. எனினும் என்றால் 'however' அல்லது 'ஆனாலும்' என்று பொருள்; இது முரண்பாட்டைக் காட்டும் இணைப்பியாகும். உதாரணமாக, "மழை பெய்தது, ஆதலால் நிலம் நனைந்தது" என்பதில் ஆதலால் இரண்டு எளிய வாக்கியங்களை இணைத்து ஒரு காரண-விளைவு வாக்கியமாக மாற்றுகிறது.

content_json.lesson_intro: Today we move from words to 'Sentences' (Thodar). In Tamil, a series of words arranged logically to convey a thought is a Thodar. We look at the basic building blocks of a sentence: Ezhuvai (Subject), Payanilai (Predicate), and Seyappaduporul (Object). We also explore different sentence types—Statement, Question, Command, and Emotion. TNPSC often asks you to identify the sentence type or change one type to another. Mastering this ensures you don't make mistakes in the 'Identification' and 'Transformation' questions.

quick_notes.title: Ettuthokai (8 Anthologies)
quick_notes.detail: 1. Natrinai. 2. Kurunthokai. 3. Akananuru. 4. Purananuru. 5. Pathitrupathu. 6. Kalithokai. 7. Aingurunuru. 8. Paripaadal. Note : Purananuru and Pathitrupathu are PURAM (History/War). Paripaadal is both Akam and Puram. Others are AKAM (Love).
quick_notes.explanation: Ettuthokai, which means the Eight Anthologies, is a collection of eight ancient Tamil poetry books. These poems were written over 2,000 years ago during the Sangam period, a time of great literary gatherings in South India. The eight books are: 1. Natrinai, 2. Kurunthokai, 3. Akananuru, 4. Purananuru, 5. Pathitrupathu, 6. Kalithokai, 7. Aingurunuru, and 8. Paripaadal. In these poems, the main theme is called Akam, which means love and personal emotions, or Puram, which means war, heroism, and public life. Specifically, Purananuru and Pathitrupathu are Puram poems about history and war, while Paripaadal contains both Akam and Puram themes. All the remaining books, including Natrinai, Kurunthokai, Akananuru, Kalithokai, and Aingurunuru, are purely Akam poems focused on love.

quick_notes.title: Pattuppattu (10 Idyls)
quick_notes.detail: Includes: 1. Thirumurugatrupadai (on Lord Murugan). 2. Porunaratrupadai. 3. Sirupanatrupadai. 4. Perumpanatrupadai. 5. Mullaippaattu (shortest). 6. Maduraikanchi (longest). 7. Nedunalvaadai. 8. Kurinchippaattu. 9. Pattinappaalai. 10. Malaipadukadaam.
quick_notes.explanation: Pattuppattu is a collection of ten long poems from the ancient Tamil Sangam literature, which was written between 300 BCE and 300 CE. The word Pattuppattu means "Ten Songs" or "Ten Idyls," and an idyl is a simple, peaceful poem describing country or village life. The first poem in this collection is Thirumurugatrupadai, which is a guide poem that praises Lord Murugan, the Hindu god of war and victory. The shortest poem in the collection is Mullaippaattu, which describes the forest region called Mullai, while the longest poem is Maduraikanchi, which describes the city of Madurai and praises the king who ruled there. The other poems include Porunaratrupadai, a guide for war drummers; Sirupanatrupadai and Perumpanatrupadai, which are guides for traveling minstrels or singers; Nedunalvaadai, which describes the cold winter season; Kurinchippaattu, which describes the mountainous region; Pattinappaalai, which describes a coastal town; and Malaipadukadaam, which describes a mountain waterfall. Each poem is a separate work that gives details about the Tamil landscape, people, and culture during the Sangam period.

quick_notes.title: Atrupadai Literature
quick_notes.detail: A genre where a poet/artist who has received gifts from a king guides another artist to the same king. "Atrupadai" means "showing the way".
quick_notes.explanation: Atrupadai Literature is a type of ancient Tamil poetry. The word Atrupadai means showing the way. In this genre, a poet or artist who has already received generous gifts from a certain king writes a poem that guides another poet or artist to go to that same king for rewards. The first poet describes the king's generosity and the route to reach him. This helped wandering artists find patrons who would support their work.

quick_notes.title: Purananuru (புறநானூறு)
quick_notes.detail: A compilation of 400 songs on external life (War, Kings, Bravery, Charity). It is the "Mirror of Tamil History". Famous line : "Yadhum Oore Yavarum Kelir" (Kaniyan Pungundranar).
quick_notes.explanation: Purananuru is a collection of 400 ancient Tamil poems from the Sangam period, which was a classical age of Tamil literature. These poems focus on external life meaning public life and activities like war, kings, bravery, and charity, as opposed to love and personal emotions. Because it accurately describes the rulers, battles, customs, and generosity of that time, it is often called the Mirror of Tamil History. One very famous line from this work is "Yadhum Oore Yavarum Kelir" written by the poet Kaniyan Pungundranar, which means "every place is my homeland and all people are my relatives."

quick_notes.title: Pathinen Keelkanakku (Minor 18)
quick_notes.detail: Composed in the post-Sangam (Didactic) period. Mostly focused on morals/ethics. Includes Thirukkural, Naaladiyar, Inna Narpathu, Iniyavai Narpathu.
quick_notes.explanation: Pathinen Keelkanakku, which translates to "The Eighteen Minor Works," is a collection of eighteen ancient Tamil texts composed after the Sangam period, in what is called the Didactic period, meaning a time focused on teaching lessons. These texts are mostly about morals and ethics, which are rules for how to live a good and honest life. The most famous text in this collection is the Thirukkural, a book of 1,330 short verses on virtue, wealth, and love. Other important works include Naaladiyar, which has 400 poems on moral conduct, Inna Narpathu, which describes forty things that cause suffering, and Iniyavai Narpathu, which lists forty things that bring happiness. Each of these works is written in simple Tamil to teach everyday people how to behave wisely and kindly.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the original structure of the Indian Constitution:
1. The original Constitution had 395 Articles and 8 Schedules.
2. Currently, the Constitution has 25 Parts and 12 Schedules.
3. The original Constitution had 22 Parts.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation: All statements are correct: original Constitution had 22 Parts, 395 Articles, 8 Schedules; current structure has 25 Parts, 448+ Articles, 12 Schedules.

questions.question:

2. Its first meeting was held on December 9, 1946.

quick_notes.title: Constitution Structure
quick_notes.detail: Original Constitution (1949): 22 Parts, 395 Articles, 8 Schedules. Current structure: 25 Parts, 448+ Articles, 12 Schedules, 5 Appendices. Common UPSC trap: "Originally how many articles?" = 395 NOT 448.
quick_notes.explanation: The Constitution of India is a written document that was created in 1949. Originally, it had 22 Parts (which are like major sections), 395 Articles (which are the individual rules or laws), and 8 Schedules (which are lists or tables attached to the Constitution, like the list of official languages). Over time, through amendments (changes), the Constitution has grown. Today, it has 25 Parts, more than 448 Articles, 12 Schedules, and 5 Appendices (additional documents at the end). A common mistake to avoid is thinking the original number of Articles was 448; it was actually 395. The number 448 refers to the current number of Articles after many amendments were added.

quick_notes.title: Key Committees
quick_notes.detail: Drafting Committee: Ambedkar. Union Powers Committee: Nehru. Union Constitution Committee: Nehru. Provincial Constitution Committee: Patel. Advisory Committee on FRs: Patel. Rules & Procedure Committee: Rajendra Prasad. Exam trap: Ambedkar: Drafting ONLY. Patel: FRs+Provincial.
quick_notes.explanation: The Constituent Assembly of India, which wrote the Constitution, set up several small groups called committees to handle different parts of the work. The Drafting Committee, led by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, was responsible for taking all the decisions from other committees and turning them into the final written document, the Constitution. The Union Powers Committee and the Union Constitution Committee, both chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru, decided how the central government (the Union) would work and what powers it would have. The Provincial Constitution Committee, chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, dealt with the structure and powers of the state governments (provinces). The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights (FR), also chaired by Patel, was in charge of listing the basic rights guaranteed to every citizen, known as Fundamental Rights. Finally, the Rules and Procedure Committee, chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad, set the rules for how the Constituent Assembly itself would run its meetings. A common mistake to avoid is thinking Ambedkar worked on many committees; he only chaired the Drafting Committee, while Patel handled both the Advisory Committee on FRs and the Provincial Constitution Committee.

quick_notes.title: Sources of Constitution
quick_notes.detail: Parliamentary system+Rule of Law: UK. Fundamental Rights+Judicial Review: USA. DPSP: Ireland. Emergency provisions: Weimar Germany. Concurrent List+Joint Sitting: Australia. Fundamental Duties: USSR. Amendment procedure Art 368: South Africa. Five Year Plans: USSR. Federal with strong Centre: Canada.
quick_notes.explanation: The Indian Constitution borrowed ideas from several countries. From the United Kingdom (UK) it took the parliamentary system, where the executive branch is part of the legislature, and the rule of law, meaning all citizens and institutions are equally subject to the law. From the United States of America (USA) it adopted Fundamental Rights (FR), which are basic individual protections enforceable in court, and Judicial Review, the power of courts to strike down laws that violate the Constitution. Ireland provided the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), which are non-binding guidelines for the government to create a just society. Germany's Weimar Constitution inspired emergency provisions, which allow the central government to assume special powers during crises. Australia contributed the Concurrent List, a set of subjects on which both the central and state governments can legislate, and the Joint Sitting of both houses of Parliament to resolve legislative deadlocks. The Soviet Union (USSR) gave the concepts of Fundamental Duties, which are citizens' obligations such as respecting the national flag, and Five Year Plans for economic planning and development. The amendment procedure under Article 368 of the Indian Constitution, which details how the Constitution can be changed, was inspired by South Africa's constitution. Finally, Canada provided the model of a federal system with a strong central government, where power is divided between the Centre and states but the Centre holds greater authority.

quick_notes.title: Twelve Schedules
quick_notes.detail: 1st: States+UTs. 2nd: Salaries(President, Governors, Judges, CAG). 3rd: Oaths. 4th: Rajya Sabha seats allocation. 5th: Scheduled Areas. 6th: Tribal Areas(NE:Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram). 7th: Union(98)+State(61)+Concurrent(52) Lists [MOST TESTED]. 8th: 22 Official Languages. 9th: Acts protected from judicial review(added by 1st Amendment 1951). 10th: Anti-defection(52nd Amendment 1985). 11th: PR 29 subjects(73rd Amendment). 12th: ULB 18 subjects(74th Amendment).
quick_notes.explanation: The twelve schedules of the Indian Constitution are appendices that provide detailed lists and rules. Schedule 1 names states and union territories (UTs); Schedule 2 fixes salaries for the President, Governors, judges, and the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG); Schedule 3 prescribes oaths; Schedule 4 allocates Rajya Sabha seats; Schedule 5 governs scheduled areas; and Schedule 6 governs tribal areas in the north-eastern states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. Schedule 7 divides lawmaking power into three lists: the Union List (98 subjects), the State List (61 subjects), and the Concurrent List (52 subjects); Schedule 8 recognizes 22 official languages; Schedule 9 shields certain laws from judicial review (the power of courts to strike down laws), added by the First Amendment of 1951; and Schedule 10 deals with anti-defection (preventing party switching) added by the 52nd Amendment of 1985. Schedule 11 lists 29 subjects for Panchayati Raj (rural local government) added by the 73rd Amendment, and Schedule 12 lists 18 subjects for urban local bodies (municipalities) added by the 74th Amendment.

content_json.lesson_intro: Before studying any individual topic in Indian Polity — Fundamental Rights, Parliament, the President — you need a mental map of the entire Constitution. Think of it like the table of contents of a massive book. The Constituent Assembly first met on December 9, 1946. By November 26, 1949, the Constitution was adopted. It came into force on January 26, 1950 — chosen to honour the 1930 Purna Swaraj declaration. The Constitution you study today is not what was adopted in 1949. The original had 395 Articles, 8 Schedules, and 22 Parts. Over 100+ amendments later: 448+ Articles, 12 Schedules, 25 Parts. UPSC tests both original and current numbers.

lesson_pages.intro: The Constitution of India is a written document that was created in 1949. snapshot.title: Fundamental Rights Block 1: Art 12–18 (Right to Equality)
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC Ranker Hook: Art 12 defines "State". Art 13 is the heart of Judicial Review. Art 14 applies to foreigners; Art 15/16 DO NOT. Art 17 is absolute. Art 18 allows military/academic titles.

quick_notes.title: Article 12 & 13: The Guardians
quick_notes.detail: Art 12: Defines "State" to include Government/Parliament, State Govts/Legislatures, Local authorities (Panchayats/Municipalities), and Statutory/Non-statutory authorities (LIC, ONGC, SAIL). Art 13: Declares that all laws inconsistent with FRs shall be void. This is the explicit basis for Judicial Review by SC (Art 32) and HC (Art 226).
quick_notes.explanation: Article 12 of the Constitution defines the term "State" for the purpose of Fundamental Rights. Under this definition, "State" includes the central Government and Parliament, the state governments and their legislatures, all local authorities like Panchayats and Municipalities, and other bodies like LIC, ONGC, or SAIL which are created by law and carry out public functions. Article 13 establishes that any law made by the State which goes against any Fundamental Right will be considered void or invalid. This means if Parliament or a state legislature passes a law that takes away your rights, the courts can throw it out. This power of courts to check laws is called Judicial Review, and it can be exercised in the Supreme Court under Article 32 or in a High Court under Article 226. Together, Articles 12 and 13 are guardians because they define who cannot violate your rights and give courts the clear power to cancel any law that does so.

quick_notes.title: Article 14: Equality Before Law
quick_notes.detail: Equality Before Law (UK origin - negative concept) + Equal Protection of Laws (USA origin - positive concept). It permits "Reasonable Classification" but prohibits "Class Legislation". Exceptions : President and Governors have immunity under Art 361.
quick_notes.explanation: Article 14 of the Indian Constitution guarantees two related rights: "Equality before the law" means that no person is above the law and every individual is subject to the same law in the same way, a concept borrowed from the United Kingdom that is considered a "negative" duty on the state not to discriminate. "Equal protection of the laws" means that the law itself must treat people in similar situations equally, a "positive" duty borrowed from the United States that requires the state to provide the same legal protection to all. This Article allows the government to make "reasonable classification", which means it can create different rules for different groups of people as long as the classification has a fair and logical basis related to the law's purpose. But it forbids "class legislation", which means making arbitrary laws that single out a specific person or group for favor or disfavor without a reasonable reason. The only exception mentioned here is that the President of India and the Governors of states have special immunity under Article 361 of the Constitution, which means they cannot be sued or prosecuted in a court of law while they are holding office. This exception exists to protect the dignity and independence of these high offices, not to give them personal privileges.

quick_notes.title: Article 15: Prohibition of Discrimination
quick_notes.detail: State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds ONLY of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth. Note the word "ONLY"—discrimination on other grounds (like residence) is permitted. Special provisions for women, children, and socially/educationally backward classes (Art 15(4) and (5)) are exceptions.
quick_notes.explanation: Article 15 of the Indian Constitution is called the Prohibition of Discrimination. It says that the State, which means all government bodies, cannot treat any citizen unfairly or unequally if the only reason is their religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. The word "only" is very important here: if the government has a different reason, such as where a person lives or their income, it is allowed to treat them differently. For example, a state can give benefits only to people who live in that state. However, the Constitution also allows the State to make special laws for women and children, as well as for socially and educationally backward classes, which include Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST). These exceptions are explained in clauses 4 and 5 of Article 15, which permit the government to reserve seats in public educational institutions for these groups.

quick_notes.title: Article 16: Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment
quick_notes.detail: No discrimination in state employment. 77th and 81st Amendments added provisions for reservation in promotion and "carry forward" rule. 103rd Amendment added 10% EWS reservation (Art 16(6)).
quick_notes.explanation: Article 16 of the Indian Constitution ensures that every citizen has equal access to jobs and posts under the government, meaning the state cannot discriminate against anyone based on religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, or residence when hiring for public employment. "Public employment" refers to jobs in government departments, public sector companies, and other state-run organisations. However, the Constitution allows the government to make special provisions for certain groups: the 77th Amendment (1995) added Article 16(4A), which permits the state to reserve seats in promotions—meaning giving preference in moving to higher positions—for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST) if they are underrepresented in government service. The 81st Amendment (2000) added Article 16(4B), which allows unfilled reserved positions from previous years—called "carry forward" rule—to be filled in later years, even if the total reserved seats exceed 50% of the available posts in that year. The 103rd Amendment (2019) added Article 16(6), which provides 10% reservation in public employment for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS)—citizens whose annual family income is less than a certain limit and who own limited agricultural land or assets, but only for those not already covered by SC, ST, or Other Backward Classes (OBC) reservations. The core principle remains that while general equality is guaranteed, the state can make targeted exceptions to uplift historically and economically disadvantaged groups.

quick_notes.title: Article 17 & 18: Social Equality
quick_notes.detail: Art 17: Abolition of Untouchability. It is an ABSOLUTE right (no exceptions). Art 18: Abolition of Titles. Military and Academic distinctions are NOT titles. Bharat Ratna/Padma awards are not titles to be used as prefixes/suffixes.
quick_notes.explanation: Article 17 and 18: Social Equality Article 17 of the Indian Constitution abolishes "untouchability," which was the cruel social practice of treating certain people as impure and outside the caste system, and it makes the practice of untouchability a punishable offense. This is an absolute right, meaning there are no exceptions or circumstances where untouchability can be practiced legally. Article 18 of the Indian Constitution abolishes "titles," which are honorary rankings like "Sir" or "Raja" that were given by the British to create a social hierarchy, but it clearly states that military and academic distinctions, such as a "Param Vir Chakra" award or a PhD degree, are not considered titles under this rule. Under Article 18, national awards like the Bharat Ratna or Padma awards are not official titles that can be used as prefixes or suffixes to a person's name, so you cannot write "Bharat Ratna Sachin Tendulkar" legally, though the award itself is honored. Both articles aim to ensure social equality by removing artificial barriers of status and hierarchy created by tradition or government.

content_json.lesson_intro: Welcome to Part III of the Constitution—the 'Magna Carta' of India. Fundamental Rights (FRs) are the most critical part of your UPSC Polity preparation because they define the relationship between the citizen and the State. We begin with the 'Right to Equality'. Before you learn about the rights themselves, you must understand Article 12 (which defines who the 'State' is) and Article 13 (which gives the courts the power of Judicial Review). Article 14 to 18 then lay the groundwork for a society free from discrimination, untouchability, and titles of nobility. For a UPSC aspirant, these aren't just articles; they are the tools used to challenge arbitrary state action.

quick_notes.title: The Amendment Map: The Big 10
quick_notes.detail: 1st (1951): 9th Schedule added. 7th (1956): Reorganization of states. 24th (1971): Parliament can amend FRs. 42nd (1976): "Mini Constitution", Socialist/Secular/Integrity, FDs added. 44th (1978): Restored rights after Emergency, Property right removed from FR. 52nd (1985): Anti-defection (10th Sch). 61st (1988): Voting age 21→18. 73rd/74th (1992): Panchayats/ULB. 86th (2002): RTE. 101st (2016): GST. 103rd (2019): EWS. 104th (2020): Anglo-Indian seats abolished.
quick_notes.explanation: The first amendment in 1951 added the Ninth Schedule, which is a special list of laws that cannot be challenged in court. The seventh amendment in 1956 reorganized the boundaries of states to match language and regional differences. The twenty-fourth amendment in 1971 gave Parliament the power to change any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights (FR), which are basic freedoms like equality and speech. The forty-second amendment in 1976 is called the "Mini Constitution"; it added the words Socialist, Secular, and Integrity to the Preamble, and also added Fundamental Duties (FD), which are responsibilities every citizen must follow. The forty-fourth amendment in 1978 removed the right to property from the list of Fundamental Rights (FR) and restored other rights that had been suspended during the Emergency period. The fifty-second amendment in 1985 added the Tenth Schedule to stop legislators from switching parties, which is called the anti-defection law. The sixty-first amendment in 1988 lowered the minimum voting age from 21 years to 18 years. The seventy-third and seventy-fourth amendments in 1992 gave constitutional status to local village councils (Panchayats) and urban local bodies (ULB), which are city governments. The eighty-sixth amendment in 2002 made the right to free and compulsory education (RTE) for children aged 6 to 14 a Fundamental Right (FR). The one hundred and first amendment in 2016 introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST), which is a single tax on most goods and services. The one hundred and third amendment in 2019 gave 10% reservation in government jobs and colleges to Economically Weaker Sections (EWS), which are citizens from poor families not covered by other quotas. The one hundred and fourth amendment in 2020 ended the reserved seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for Anglo-Indian community members.

quick_notes.title: Procedure for Amendment (Art 368)
quick_notes.detail: Initiated ONLY in Parliament (not State Legislatures). No prior permission of President. Simple majority, whereas Special majority, whereas Special majority + State ratification (for federal features). President MUST give assent to Constitution Amendment Bill (24th Amendment).
quick_notes.explanation: The procedure to change the Constitution is written in Article 368. An amendment can only be started in Parliament, not in any State Legislature, and the President's prior permission is not needed to introduce the bill. There are three different ways to pass an amendment depending on what part of the Constitution is being changed. For most ordinary matters, the bill needs a simple majority, which means more than half of the members present and voting in each house must agree. For more important changes, a special majority is required, meaning at least two-thirds of the members present and voting, and also a majority of the total membership of each house must approve. For changes that affect federal features, like the powers of states or the Supreme Court, the bill needs that same special majority in Parliament plus ratification by at least half of the state legislatures. Once the bill is passed correctly, the President must give their assent to it, meaning they cannot send it back or refuse it, and this rule was made clear by the 24th Amendment to the Constitution.
